name: PHP
title: PHP from the first echo
intro: PHP started in 1994 as a few tools for a personal home page and became the language behind a large share of the web, including WordPress and the early Facebook. A web server runs a PHP script each time a page is asked for, and whatever the script prints becomes the page. Modern PHP (version 8) has types, classes, enums and fast arrow functions, and it also runs fine from the command line, which is how these lessons use it. Every example is a whole script and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, save it as hello.php and type php hello.php.

sections.p: A PHP file starts with <?php. Anything before that tag would be sent out as plain text, which is how PHP mixes into web pages. echo prints, and statements end with a semicolon. Nothing ends the line unless you print "\n".
sections.code:
<?php
echo "Hello, squirrel!\n";
echo "Nuts: ", 42, "\n";

sections.p: Every variable name starts with $, and you don't declare a type: the value carries it. The dot . joins strings. Inside double quotes a variable is replaced by its value; inside single quotes the text is kept exactly as written.
sections.code:
<?php
$name = "Hazel";
$nuts = 7;
echo "Hi, " . $name . "!\n";
echo "$name has $nuts nuts\n";
echo '$name has $nuts nuts', "\n";
sections.out:
Hi, Hazel!
Hazel has 7 nuts
$name has $nuts nuts

options:
Up the oak
Up the oak
practice.why: Double quotes put the variable's value in. Single quotes print the text exactly as written.
The dot joins text. + adds numbers.

practice.q: What does every PHP variable name start with?
practice.why: The $ tells PHP the word is a variable, which is also how it can spot variables inside double-quoted strings.

lessons.title: Types and comparing
lessons.summary: int, float, string, bool, null, == and ===.

sections.p: PHP's basic types are int, float, string, bool and null. / gives a float when the division isn't exact; intdiv keeps only the whole part and % gives the remainder. var_dump shows a value together with its type, which is handy when something surprises you.
sections.code:
<?php
var_dump(17 / 5);
var_dump(10 / 5);
var_dump(intdiv(17, 5));
var_dump(17 % 5);
var_dump("nuts");
var_dump(null);
sections.out:
float(3.4)
int(2)
int(3)
int(2)
string(4) "nuts"
NULL

sections.p: == converts the two sides to a common type before comparing, so the string "5" equals the number 5. === also checks that the types match. Most PHP style guides say to use === unless you mean to convert. var_dump on a comparison shows bool(true) or bool(false).
sections.code:
<?php
var_dump("5" == 5);
var_dump("5" === 5);
var_dump(0 == "");
var_dump(null == false);
var_dump(null === false);

sections.p: Arithmetic on a string that holds a number turns it into that number first, so "4" + 3 is 7. (int) converts on purpose. The ?? operator gives a fallback when a value is null or missing.
sections.code:
<?php
echo "4" + 3, "\n";
echo (int) "12 acorns", "\n";
$found = null;
echo $found ?? "nothing yet", "\n";

practice.why: An exact division of two ints stays an int. When it doesn't come out even, the result is a float.
Both strings look like numbers, so == compares them as numbers, and 1e1 is 10. === compares the strings as written, and they differ.

lessons.title: Decisions and loops
lessons.summary: if, elseif, match, for and while.

sections.p: if, elseif and else choose a block to run. && means and, || means or and ! means not. A match expression picks a value by comparing with ===, and gives an error if nothing matches and there is no default.
sections.code:
<?php
$nuts = 12;
if ($nuts > 20) {
    echo "feast\n";
} elseif ($nuts > 10) {
    echo "good day\n";
} else {
    echo "keep looking\n";
}
$day = "sat";
echo match ($day) {
    "sat", "sun" => "nap in the drey",
    "mon" => "bury nuts",
    default => "forage",
}, "\n";
sections.out:
good day
nap in the drey

sections.p: for has a start, a test and a step. while repeats while its test holds. break leaves a loop early and continue skips to the next pass.
sections.code:
<?php
for ($i = 1; $i <= 5; $i++) {
    if ($i === 3) {
        continue;
    }
    echo $i, " ";
}
echo "\n";
$height = 1;
while ($height < 20) {
    $height *= 3;
}
echo $height, "\n";

practice.why: match compares with ===, so the string "2" only matches the string case.
The loop adds 1, 2, 3 and 4, then break stops it when i reaches 5.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: Lists, key–value arrays, foreach and the array functions.

sections.p: A PHP array does two jobs. Written with plain values, ["oak", "ash"], it is a list numbered from 0. $list[] = ... adds to the end and count gives the size. foreach visits every item; implode joins them into one string.
sections.code:
<?php
$trees = ["oak", "ash"];
$trees[] = "hazel";
echo count($trees), " ", $trees[0], "\n";
foreach ($trees as $i => $tree) {
    echo "$i: $tree\n";
}
echo implode(", ", $trees), "\n";
sections.out:
3 oak
0: oak
1: ash
2: hazel
oak, ash, hazel

sections.p: Written with key => value pairs, the same array type works as a dictionary. The array keeps the order you put things in. isset checks whether a key is there, and ksort sorts by key.
sections.code:
<?php
$stash = ["oak" => 4, "hazel" => 9];
$stash["beech"] = 2;
$stash["oak"] += 1;
foreach ($stash as $tree => $nuts) {
    echo "$tree: $nuts\n";
}
var_dump(isset($stash["pine"]));
ksort($stash);
echo implode(" ", array_keys($stash)), "\n";
sections.out:
oak: 5
hazel: 9
beech: 2
bool(false)
beech hazel oak

sections.p: PHP has a long list of built-in array functions. array_filter keeps items that pass a test, array_map changes each item, and array_sum adds them up. The test or change is a small function, written here as an arrow function fn($n) => $n * 2. array_filter keeps the original keys; array_values renumbers them from 0.
sections.code:
<?php
$nuts = [5, 12, 3, 8, 20];
$big = array_filter($nuts, fn($n) => $n > 4);
$doubled = array_map(fn($n) => $n * 2, $big);
echo implode(" ", $doubled), "\n";
echo implode(",", array_keys($big)), "\n";
echo implode(",", array_keys(array_values($big))), "\n";
echo array_sum($nuts), "\n";

practice.why: $a[] = adds at the next index, 2, so there are three items and $a[2] is z.
Hazel goes from 3 to 4, and 4 + 1 is 5.

practice.q: What does array_filter do with the keys of the items it keeps?
practice.why: That is why the lesson uses array_values when it wants a list numbered from 0 again.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: Typed parameters, defaults, named arguments and closures.

sections.p: function defines a function. Parameters can have types and a default value, and : int after the brackets gives the return type. With declare(strict_types=1); at the top of the file, passing the wrong type is an error instead of a silent conversion. Named arguments let you pass values by name, in any order.
sections.code:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function share(int $nuts, int $squirrels = 2): int {
    return intdiv($nuts, $squirrels);
}

echo share(10), "\n";
echo share(10, 3), "\n";
echo share(squirrels: 5, nuts: 20), "\n";

sections.p: A function can be a value stored in a variable. An anonymous function must list outside variables it wants with use; an arrow function fn sees them automatically. Either kind can be passed to another function.
sections.code:
<?php
$bonus = 3;
$addBonus = function ($n) use ($bonus) {
    return $n + $bonus;
};
$triple = fn($n) => $n * 3;

function twice(callable $f, int $x): int {
    return $f($f($x));
}

echo $addBonus(4), "\n";
echo twice($triple, 2), "\n";
echo twice($addBonus, 0), "\n";

practice.code:
<?php
function greet(string $name, string $greeting = "Hello"): string {
    return "$greeting, $name";
}
echo greet("Hazel"), "\n";
echo greet(greeting: "Hi", name: "Acorn");
practice.why: The first call uses the default greeting. The second names both arguments, so the order doesn't matter.
An arrow function copies the outside value when it is created. Changing $n later doesn't affect it.

lessons.title: Classes and enums
lessons.summary: Constructor promotion, readonly properties, interfaces and enums.

sections.p: A class groups data (properties) with the functions that work on it (methods). -> reaches a property or calls a method on an object, and $this is the object the method was called on. Writing private int $nuts = 0 in the constructor's brackets declares the property and sets it in one go; this is called constructor promotion. A readonly property can be set once and never changed.
sections.code:
<?php
class Squirrel {
    public function __construct(
        public readonly string $name,
        private int $nuts = 0,
    ) {}

    public function gather(int $found): void {
        $this->nuts += $found;
    }

    public function report(): string {
        return "{$this->name} has {$this->nuts}";
    }
}

$s = new Squirrel("Hazel");
$s->gather(3);
$s->gather(4);
echo $s->report(), "\n";
echo $s->name, "\n";

sections.p: An interface lists methods a class promises to have. Code that takes the interface type works with any class that implements it, and each class answers in its own way.
sections.code:
<?php
interface Animal {
    public function sound(): string;
}

class Squirrel implements Animal {
    public function sound(): string { return "chitter"; }
}

class Owl implements Animal {
    public function sound(): string { return "hoo"; }
}

function chorus(Animal ...$animals): string {
    return implode(" ", array_map(fn(Animal $a) => $a->sound(), $animals));
}

echo chorus(new Squirrel(), new Owl(), new Squirrel()), "\n";

sections.p: An enum is a type with a fixed set of cases. A backed enum gives each case a string or int value, and from turns a value back into its case. Enums can have methods, and match on an enum reads well.
sections.code:
<?php
enum Season: string {
    case Spring = "spring";
    case Autumn = "autumn";

    public function job(): string {
        return match ($this) {
            Season::Spring => "find new shoots",
            Season::Autumn => "bury nuts",
        };
    }
}

$s = Season::from("autumn");
echo $s->name, "\n";
echo $s->value, "\n";
echo $s->job(), "\n";

practice.code:
<?php
class Counter {
    private int $count = 0;
    public function tick(): static {
        $this->count++;
        return $this;
    }
    public function value(): int { return $this->count; }
}
echo (new Counter())->tick()->tick()->tick()->value();
practice.why: tick returns the same object, so the calls chain. Three ticks make the count 3.

practice.q: What happens when code tries to change a readonly property after the constructor set it?
practice.why: readonly means one assignment only. A second one stops the script with an Error unless it is caught.

sections.p: On a web page, text a visitor typed must never be printed straight into HTML, or a name like <script> becomes code in everyone else's browser. htmlspecialchars turns the special characters into HTML entities so they show as text. This one habit stops a whole family of attacks.
sections.code: Hazel & "friends"'; echo htmlspecialchars($typed), "\n";

sections.p: json_encode turns arrays into JSON, the format web apps send back and forth: lists become [...] and key–value arrays become {...}. printf fills a template: %s for a string, %d for a whole number, %.2f for a number with two decimals, and %5d pads to five places.
sections.code:
<?php
echo json_encode(["name" => "Hazel", "nuts" => [3, 4]]), "\n";
echo json_encode(["oak", "ash"]), "\n";
printf("%s paid %.2f for %d nuts\n", "Acorn", 1.5, 6);
printf("[%5d]\n", 42);

practice.why: < becomes <, which a browser shows as < without treating it as the start of a tag.
%.1f rounds to one decimal place, and %3d pads 7 on the left to three characters.

lessons.title: Errors and exceptions
lessons.summary: try, catch, finally, and your own Exception subclasses.

sections.p: When something goes wrong, PHP throws an exception and the script stops unless a try block catches it. Catch the most specific type first: InvalidArgumentException before the general Exception. A finally block runs whether or not anything was thrown, which is useful for cleanup that must always happen.
sections.code:
<?php
function take(int $stored, int $asked): int {
    if ($asked < 0) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException("asked must be non-negative");
    }
    if ($asked > $stored) {
        throw new Exception("asked for $asked, only $stored stored");
    }
    return $stored - $asked;
}

foreach ([3, 12, -1] as $asked) {
    try {
        $left = take(10, $asked);
        echo "left: $left\n";
    } catch (InvalidArgumentException $e) {
        echo "bad input: ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
    } catch (Exception $e) {
        echo "refused: ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
    } finally {
        echo "checked $asked\n";
    }
}
sections.out:
left: 7
checked 3
refused: asked for 12, only 10 stored
checked 12
bad input: asked must be non-negative
checked -1

sections.p: A class that extends Exception can carry extra fields, and instanceof (or a typed catch) tells your failures apart from everyone else's. Call parent::__construct so the message and stack trace are set up properly.
sections.code:
<?php
class StashFullError extends Exception {
    public function __construct(public readonly int $limit) {
        parent::__construct("the stash holds at most $limit nuts");
    }
}

function store(array &$stash, string $nut, int $limit = 2): void {
    if (count($stash) >= $limit) {
        throw new StashFullError($limit);
    }
    $stash[] = $nut;
}

$stash = [];
try {
    store($stash, "acorn");
    store($stash, "walnut");
    store($stash, "pecan");
} catch (StashFullError $e) {
    echo $e::class, " ", $e->limit, " ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
}
echo implode(", ", $stash), "\n";
sections.out:
StashFullError 2 the stash holds at most 2 nuts
acorn, walnut

sections.p: PHP has no try-with-resources, but finally is the usual place to close what you opened. It runs even when the try throws, so a later catch still sees a tidy state.
sections.code:
<?php
function dig(string $spot): void {
    echo "open $spot\n";
    try {
        if ($spot === "south") {
            throw new RuntimeException("roof fell in");
        }
        echo "working\n";
    } finally {
        echo "close $spot\n";
    }
}

try {
    dig("north");
    dig("south");
} catch (RuntimeException $e) {
    echo "caught: ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
}
sections.out:
open north
working
close north
open south
close south
caught: roof fell in

practice.code:
<?php
try {
    echo "a\n";
    throw new Exception("x");
    echo "b\n";
} catch (Exception $e) {
    echo "c\n";
} finally {
    echo "d\n";
}
practice.why: The throw skips b; the catch runs, then finally always runs.

practice.code:
<?php
class Oops extends Exception {}
try {
    throw new Oops("late");
} catch (Oops $e) {
    echo $e instanceof Exception ? "yes" : "no";
}
practice.why: An Oops is also an Exception, because Oops extends Exception.

options: The first matching catch wins, so the specific type must come first
Exception cannot be caught at all
finally only runs for the first catch
practice.answer: The first matching catch wins, so the specific type must come first
practice.why: InvalidArgumentException is a subclass of Exception, so a bare catch (Exception) would swallow it first.

lessons.title: Strings in depth
lessons.summary: substr, strpos, explode/implode, sprintf and replace.

sections.p: Beyond joining with ., PHP has a long list of string functions. substr cuts a piece (a negative start counts from the end), strpos finds a substring and returns false when it is missing — compare with ===, because position 0 is also falsy. explode splits and implode joins; sprintf fills a template the same way printf does, but returns the string.
sections.code:
<?php
$s = "hazelnut stash";
echo substr($s, 0, 5), " ", substr($s, -5), "\n";
echo strpos($s, "nut"), " ", (strpos($s, "oak") === false ? "missing" : "found"), "\n";
echo implode("-", explode(" ", $s)), "\n";
echo sprintf("%-9s %3d %.1f%%", "acorn", 12, 66.666), "\n";
echo str_replace("nut", "seed", $s), "\n";
sections.out:
hazel stash
5 missing
hazelnut-stash
acorn      12 66.7%
hazelseed stash

sections.p: preg_split splits on a regular expression, which is handy when the separators have uneven spaces. str_ireplace replaces without caring about case, and array_reverse flips a list before you join it back.
sections.code:
<?php
$csv = "acorn, walnut, pecan ,  hazelnut";
$nuts = preg_split('/\s*,\s*/', $csv);
echo implode(" | ", array_reverse($nuts)), "\n";
echo sprintf("[%04d] %s", 7, strtoupper("ok")), "\n";
$note = "Oak oak OAK";
echo str_ireplace("oak", "elm", $note), "\n";
sections.out:
hazelnut | pecan | walnut | acorn
[0007] OK
elm elm elm

sections.p: trim strips spaces from both ends, strlen counts bytes (fine for plain ASCII), and str_contains is the clear yes/no test for a substring when you don't need the position.
sections.code:
<?php
$line = "  up   the   tree ";
$words = preg_split('/\s+/', trim($line));
echo count($words), ": ", implode("|", $words), "\n";
echo strlen("squirrel"), " ", (str_contains("squirrel", "quir") ? "yes" : "no"), "\n";

practice.why: From index 2, take 3 characters for cde; -2 takes the last two.
Position 0 is found, but 0 is falsy, so ? treats it as no. === false is the reliable test.
explode cuts on -, implode glues with :.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files
lessons.summary: file_get_contents, file_put_contents, file() and JSON on disk.

sections.p: The simplest way to work with a whole file is file_put_contents to write and file_get_contents to read. file returns the lines as an array; FILE_IGNORE_NEW_LINES drops the trailing newlines. Paths are relative to the current working directory.
sections.code:
<?php
file_put_contents("stash.txt", "acorn 6\nhazelnut 2\nwalnut 1\n");
$text = file_get_contents("stash.txt");
echo "bytes: ", strlen($text), "\n";
foreach (file("stash.txt", FILE_IGNORE_NEW_LINES) as $line) {
    [$nut, $n] = explode(" ", $line);
    echo "$nut => $n\n";
}
copy("stash.txt", "backup.txt");
echo is_file("backup.txt") ? "backup ready\n" : "missing\n";
sections.out:
bytes: 28
acorn => 6
hazelnut => 2
walnut => 1
backup ready

sections.p: Pass FILE_APPEND to add to the end instead of replacing. file_exists asks whether a path is there at all; is_file asks specifically for a regular file.
sections.code:
<?php
file_put_contents("log.txt", "day 1: found 3\n");
file_put_contents("log.txt", "day 2: found 5\n", FILE_APPEND);
echo file_get_contents("log.txt");
echo file_exists("nope.txt") ? "yes" : "no", "\n";

sections.p: Web apps often store structured data as JSON. Encode an array, write the file, then json_decode(..., true) to get an associative array back.
sections.code:
<?php
$data = ["name" => "Hazel", "nuts" => ["acorn" => 4, "walnut" => 2]];
file_put_contents("hazel.json", json_encode($data));
$back = json_decode(file_get_contents("hazel.json"), true);
echo $back["name"], " total ", array_sum($back["nuts"]), "\n";

practice.why: Two lines, a and b; FILE_IGNORE_NEW_LINES only strips the newlines, it doesn't drop empty trailing pieces here.
FILE_APPEND adds y after the existing x.

practice.q: What does json_decode($text, true) return for a JSON object?
practice.why: The second argument true asks for arrays instead of objects.

lessons.title: Project: a tagged nut inventory
lessons.summary: Enums, classes and match build a small event-sourced stash.

sections.p: An inventory is built by replaying a list of events. Each event holds a kind string, a backed NutKind enum and a count. Applying an event either updates the stock or returns an error string — a tiny tagged-union style, without throwing. A gift that asks for more walnuts than you have is skipped and reported; the rest become a sorted table.
sections.code:
<?php
enum NutKind: string {
    case Acorn = "acorn";
    case Walnut = "walnut";
    case Hazelnut = "hazelnut";
}

final class InventoryEvent {
    public function __construct(
        public readonly string $kind,
        public readonly NutKind $nut,
        public readonly int $count,
        public readonly ?string $to = null,
    ) {}
}

final class Inventory {
    /** @var array<string, int> */
    private array $stock;

    public function __construct() {
        $this->stock = array_fill_keys(
            array_map(fn(NutKind $n) => $n->value, NutKind::cases()),
            0,
        );
    }

    public function apply(InventoryEvent $e): ?string {
        $key = $e->nut->value;
        if ($e->kind === "found") {
            $this->stock[$key] += $e->count;
            return null;
        }
        if ($this->stock[$key] < $e->count) {
            return "cannot {$e->kind} {$e->count} $key: only {$this->stock[$key]}";
        }
        $this->stock[$key] -= $e->count;
        return null;
    }

    public function report(): void {
        $rows = $this->stock;
        arsort($rows);
        foreach ($rows as $nut => $n) {
            printf("%-9s %2d\n", $nut, $n);
        }
    }
}

$events = [
    new InventoryEvent("found", NutKind::Acorn, 8),
    new InventoryEvent("found", NutKind::Walnut, 3),
    new InventoryEvent("ate", NutKind::Acorn, 2),
    new InventoryEvent("gift", NutKind::Walnut, 5, "Pip"),
    new InventoryEvent("found", NutKind::Hazelnut, 4),
    new InventoryEvent("gift", NutKind::Acorn, 1, "Pip"),
];

$inv = new Inventory();
$gifts = [];
foreach ($events as $e) {
    $err = $inv->apply($e);
    if ($err !== null) {
        echo "skipped: $err\n";
        continue;
    }
    if ($e->kind === "gift") {
        $gifts[$e->to] = true;
    }
}
$inv->report();
echo "gifts to: ", implode(", ", array_keys($gifts)), "\n";
sections.out:
skipped: cannot gift 5 walnut: only 3
acorn      5
hazelnut   4
walnut     3
gifts to: Pip

sections.p: Turn the kind string into its own enum and match on it, read the events from a JSON file with file_get_contents, or keep a history of every stock along the way.

practice.q: Why does apply return ?string instead of throwing?
options: So a bad event can be skipped and reported without stopping the whole replay
PHP cannot throw inside a class
null means success only for enums
practice.answer: So a bad event can be skipped and reported without stopping the whole replay
practice.why: Returning an error value keeps the loop in charge, the same idea as a Result type.

practice.code:
<?php
enum Nut: string { case A = "acorn"; case W = "walnut"; }
$stock = array_fill_keys(array_map(fn(Nut $n) => $n->value, Nut::cases()), 0);
$stock["acorn"] += 3;
echo implode(",", array_keys($stock)), " ", $stock["acorn"];
practice.why: cases() gives both enums, value is the backing string, and acorn is then increased.

practice.q: What does arsort do before the report prints?
options: Sorts the stock by count, largest first, keeping the nut names as keys
Converts the array to a list
practice.answer: Sorts the stock by count, largest first, keeping the nut names as keys
practice.why: arsort is a reverse sort by value that preserves keys.
